j.learned_fact: Young children have twenty baby teeth; they fall out when ready and bigger teeth grow in.
j.thinking_skill: Accepting delayed gratification after understanding a cause (the tooth comes out when ready)
j.notes: Very slight; the 'wonder' moment is a tooth that was already loose in the first paragraph. Mom's fact is stated plainly but briefly.

j.thinking_skill: asking for help politely when a goal is out of reach
j.notes: A manners lesson with no factual content; the helper praising 'good asking for help' makes the moral explicit, and 'some were messy and mixed up' is a stray detail.

j.learned_fact: Round wheels roll smoothly; wheels with corners bump and stop.
j.thinking_skill: comparing two shapes' behaviour and generalising
j.notes: The cookie analogy is false: square cookies do not come out with 'bumpy, broken edges' because they have corners, so the lesson 'round is better' is taught through something untrue.

j.learned_fact: With a pulley, pulling down on one end of the rope makes the load on the other end go up.
j.thinking_skill: replicating a demonstrated mechanism on his own
j.notes: Dylan's own build has a rope and a flag but no wheel, so it is not a pulley; 'took a calm breath' is planted and the prose is flat.

j.learned_fact: Practising a rhythm slowly first and then faster helps you learn it.
j.thinking_skill: imitating and repeating a pattern
j.notes: Almost no content beyond 'practice makes progress'; the First/Next/Then/Last scaffold reads as a checklist.

j.learned_fact: A refrigerator moves heat out of its inside and releases it at the back, which is why the back feels warm.
j.thinking_skill: noticing a contrast (cold front, warm back) and asking why
j.notes: Raphael simply 'realized' the fridge pumps heat out with no reasoning or help, so the conclusion is unearned; 'That was the correct way it worked' is a planted vocabulary word, and the text is simpler than a 2nd-grade target.

j.thinking_skill: proposing a fairness rule to resolve a group conflict
j.notes: 'Landmarks need both tall buildings and wide open spaces' is a nonsensical analogy built around a planted vocabulary word; the resolution (Coach 'listened' and everything was fixed by Thursday) is a bolted-on moral with no concrete mechanism.

j.learned_fact: Sound travels into the ear and makes tiny parts inside vibrate, and louder sounds make them vibrate more.
j.thinking_skill: Controlled comparison (quiet snap vs loud snap) to test a hypothesis about loudness
j.notes: The 'which sport am I better at' setup is abandoned, and the ear explanation stays vague (no eardrum, no bones named). Feeling 'something inside vibrating' from a finger snap is dubious.

j.learned_fact: Some pines have cones sealed shut with resin that only open and release their seeds when a wildfire's heat melts the seal, so seedlings carpet a burned forest the next year.
j.thinking_skill: inferring a mechanism by comparing two specimens with a before/after photo
j.notes: One garbled sentence ('didn't have seeds because the fire had destroyed them') contradicts the point it is making; otherwise a clean discovery story with the librarian only nudging.

j.learned_fact: Earth is closest to the Sun in early January, so winter is caused by the tilt of Earth's axis: a low sun spreads its light over more ground, like a tilted flashlight, so it heats less.
j.thinking_skill: Refuting a hypothesis with data and proposing an alternative mechanism (angle of incidence) supported by an analogy
j.notes: 'He looked almost vulnerable' and the closing 'How would you paraphrase...' are forced vocabulary insertions, and the tablet conveniently confirms the tilt answer. Reads a touch young for 6th grade.

j.learned_fact: Sound waves from an approaching source are compressed (higher pitch) and from a receding source are stretched (lower pitch): the Doppler effect. Inaccuracies: the pitch does not keep climbing as a car approaches, it is steadily higher and then drops as it passes; the claim that this is 'the same principle' chemists use to study molecules is vague to the point of being misleading.
j.thinking_skill: connecting an experimental observation to an explanation and then transferring it to a new case (the recycling truck)
j.notes: The setup (dad driving in circles with the alarm on to test 'chemistry') is contrived, the physics is delivered as a bedtime explanation by mom, and 'vigorous spark' and 'sent him a signal' are forced vocabulary.

j.learned_fact: Touchscreens respond to bare fingertips but not to ordinary gloves.
j.thinking_skill: a controlled on/off experiment to isolate the cause
j.notes: Eli never learns why gloves fail (no mention of conductivity or capacitance), so the takeaway is only the symptom; 'become a herbivore and only respond to plants' misuses the vocabulary word as a non-joke, and 'robust in her opinions' is strained. The final text to Marcus ('why does your phone work with gloves') contradicts everything before it.

j.learned_fact: Regression to the mean: an unusually good or bad result is often followed by a more ordinary one, so a single drop or rebound does not prove anything changed; you need many observations over time.
j.thinking_skill: Recognizing regression to the mean and proposing longitudinal evidence to distinguish it from real change
j.notes: Alexander's own data confounds effort with luck (he did study less for the 84), so his conclusion is under-supported; the class discussion mirroring his problem is convenient. 'Improving his recovery' is garbled and the ending is a cliché.

j.learned_fact: When a country's currency weakens, imports and foreign travel cost more in that currency while its exports become cheaper for foreign buyers, so exporters gain and importers lose.
j.thinking_skill: tracing one cause to opposite effects on two parties and weighing the trade-off
j.notes: Mom's explanation carries most of the concept and the 'thirty percent more than last month' figure is implausibly large for a currency move; 'apparatus of trade' is stiff. Grace's own verification (hotel prices) is a good touch.

j.learned_fact: Winds carry millions of tons of Saharan dust across the Atlantic each year, and the phosphorus in it fertilizes the phosphorus-poor soils of the Amazon.
j.thinking_skill: Counterfactual testing: removing one input (Saharan phosphorus) from a nutrient-balance model to see whether the system still holds
j.notes: Prose and sentence structure read as middle-school, below a 16-year-old's level, and the 'model' Colton builds in an evening is hand-waved ('the numbers collapsed'). The teacher's closing 'that's how scientists actually work' is a bolted-on moral; 'lavish complexity' is a forced word choice.

j.learned_fact: Price depends on scarcity relative to demand, not on usefulness: water is cheap because it is plentiful even though one bottle is worth everything to someone dying of thirst, while diamonds are dear because few exist and many want them (the diamond-water paradox).
j.thinking_skill: reconciling two apparently contradictory observations through marginal reasoning
j.notes: The concept is delivered in a long explanatory speech from Marcus, and 'Devon sounded impetuous' is a slightly off use of the word; the hiker and Mrs. Chen vignettes are good evidence-gathering.

j.learned_fact: Radiocarbon dating works on once-living material, the half-life of carbon-14 is about 5,700 years, and the method reaches back about 50,000 years. But the story's conclusion is false: wood dated to 1962 does not contradict a guitar being bought in 1969 (wood is cut and seasoned before an instrument is built), and the claim that the half-life makes recent decades 'pretty precise' is wrong (any precision for 1960s wood comes from bomb-pulse calibration, not the half-life).
j.thinking_skill: weighing family legend against physical evidence (but drawing an invalid inference from it)
j.notes: The central inference is broken: the lab result the story treats as debunking the legend is fully consistent with it. 'He acquiesce to the idea' is ungrammatical, and Marcus delivers the carbon-dating facts as a mini-lecture.

j.learned_fact: Simpson's paradox: aggregated data can show a trend that reverses when broken down by group. BUT the numbers do not add up: 'forty-eight percent women and fifty-two percent women' is garbled; engineering is said to have 44% women applicants and then 27 of 48 (56%); the selective programs (applied math 31/180 women) have FEW women, which is the opposite of what the paradox needs.
j.thinking_skill: Disaggregating data by group to detect a reversal between aggregate and subgroup trends
j.notes: The internal figures contradict the explanation the story reaches, so a careful reader cannot reconstruct the paradox. 'The pragmatism of a conciliatory visualization' is purple and semantically empty.

j.learned_fact: The first mobile phone call was made in 1973 on a Motorola prototype weighing about 1.1 kg; a decade later the consumer version sold for nearly 4,000 dollars.
j.thinking_skill: historical empathy: reconstructing what a technology meant in its own era instead of judging it by today's standards
j.notes: 'Turgid with August heat' is a misuse (turgid means swollen or pompous, not sultry) and the 'cost less than a textbook' aside is clumsy; the classroom exercise itself is convincing and the facts check out.

j.learned_fact: The first web page went online at CERN in 1991, and in 1993 Berners-Lee persuaded CERN to release the technology royalty-free; also, a loop over ten items runs from index 0 to 9 (off-by-one error).
j.thinking_skill: Counterfactual reasoning about what a licensed web would have meant for access and learning
j.notes: The kitchen conversation is on-the-nose, and Keisha's 'he gave away his company' goes uncorrected (there was no company). 'Annuity' and 'aggrandize' are forced but used correctly.

j.learned_fact: Follower counts say little about how many people someone actually has two-way conversations with.
j.thinking_skill: reframing a failed hypothesis into a measurable question about the gap itself
j.notes: 'Historicize her approach' is a misuse (historicize does not mean break into steps) and 'a sullen quality' is odd; scraping classmates' messages at midnight passes without comment, and no verifiable fact is offered, only the story's own invented numbers.
